signals.title: AgentsDock: An IDE designed for agentic AI research

assessment.rule: Operational system not in the catalog
assessment.finding: AgentsDock describes itself as "An IDE designed for agentic AI research. AgentsDock currently supports Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor in one desktop and mobile workspace." It ships downloads for macOS, iPhone/iPad, Linux, Windows, and Android, and the setup section reads "Set up your server with a few simple commands", "Access the server from any device", "Have your agents do research and model training for you", installed by cloning https://github.com/ZhengyiLuo/AgentsServer. Scope and licensing flags: the page labels itself "Open source · Beta testing now" but the bundled portion names no license, so the license must come from the repository, not this page; the bundled text is truncated partway through the install instructions, and much of what was read is repeated user testimonials rather than documentation. No record, candidate, or exclusion named AgentsDock exists. Boundary question: is AgentsDock an operational system in its own right, or a remote desktop/mobile front end over third-party agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) that the Atlas already records, in which case it may not warrant a separate record?

signals.title: Align AI and Mathematics–To Something Else
Apple wants to train AI on your private personal data

assessment.rule: Uncovered assistant stack behind a model release
assessment.finding: Apple's research post introduces "our third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), a family of five foundation models custom-built in collaboration with Google", spanning on-device models and server models on Private Cloud Compute, built "to unlock a wide range of helpful experiences for our users, like an entirely new Siri and intelligent tools that make everyday apps smarter". AFM 3 Cloud Pro "powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning." Flags: the page is a model and training overview dated June 8, 2026, not product documentation for Siri or Apple Intelligence, so it cannot on its own establish a product boundary; it offers no weights, API, or license terms in the bundled portion; and the text is truncated at the Evaluation section. The HN title claims Apple wants to train on private data, while the page states "We do not use our users' private personal data or user interactions when training our foundation models" — a mismatch a reviewer should not carry forward. Neither Apple Intelligence nor Siri has a record, candidate, or exclusion. Boundary question: is the reviewable thing the Apple Intelligence/Siri assistant (needing first-party product evidence beyond this page), or only a proprietary model family with no public access, which would fall to the model pipeline or outside the Atlas entirely?
